pages.x: Bioswale | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Bioswale A planted channel that slows, filters and soaks in street runoff Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 3 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Bioswale A swale takes in curb runoff. Concept sketch. Type Green infrastructure Related term Rain garden, bioretention [1] Valley example Elmer Avenue, Sun Valley [2] Reported capacity 24 swales treat 115,000 gal [2] Related Permeable paving Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is Case: Elmer Avenue Applying it to a parking lot See also Notes What it is # A bioswale is a shallow planted channel or bed that takes in runoff from a road, roof or lot and lets it soak into the ground. It is a close relative of the rain garden. The EPA describes a rain garden as a depressed area in the landscape that collects rain from a roof, driveway or street and lets it soak in, planted with grasses and flowering perennials. It can also filter pollutants and shelter wildlife. More complex versions with drainage systems and amended soils are often called bioretention. [1] Case: Elmer Avenue # Elmer Avenue in Sun Valley was a street with no pedestrian or stormwater infrastructure and frequent flooding. The retrofit captures and filters runoff from a 40-acre area. [2] The project reports: 24 bioswales that together can capture and treat 115,000 gallons of runoff and add 1,728 square feet of planting. Up to 5.4 million gallons of stormwater infiltrated per year, and reduced lead, copper and suspended solids concentrations by 60%, 33% and 18%. 23 native trees along the sidewalks. Residents satisfied with the block’s walkability rising from under 2% of survey respondents in 2006 to 92% in 2011. Those are figures reported by the project’s case study brief, not independent audits. The survey is also small and self-reported. [2] Applying it to a parking lot # In my Topanga Willows study I turn the strip where car noses overhang at the edge of a lot into a swale, with curb cuts that let runoff in. [3] That is a concept, drawn from a street-scale precedent: Elmer Avenue is a residential street, not a retail lot, and I do not know how the soil under any Woodland Hills lot drains. A percolation test would come before any design is real. Type Paving strategy Mechanisms Reflect more sun, evaporate water, or both [1] Arizona pilot Asphalt up to 152°F; cool pavement 10–16°F cooler [1] LA program 175+ lane miles [2] Main caution Can feel hotter to pedestrians [2] Figures link to Notes below. Contents What it is Los Angeles’s experience My working rule What I do not know See also Notes What it is # The EPA uses cool pavement for paving materials that reflect more solar energy, enhance water evaporation, or have otherwise been modified to stay cooler than conventional pavements. It can be made with ordinary asphalt and concrete, with coatings, or with grass paving. [1] A pilot study in Arizona found conventional paving such as asphalt reaching surface temperatures up to 152°F at midday, while cool pavements stayed 10 to 16°F cooler. [1] Los Angeles’s experience # Los Angeles has spent millions installing “cool” pavement on more than 175 lane miles across the city. [2] But a UCLA study discussed by NBC Los Angeles says more research is needed to know the real benefits: cool pavement may lower surface temperatures yet feel hotter to a person, in part because the effect of sunlight is increased as heat re-radiates from the pavement. [2] I read that as a lesson in what to measure. Surface temperature is easy to read with a thermometer; comfort depends on air temperature, wind, humidity and radiation from every surface around a person. My working rule # This is my design judgment, not a sourced finding: shade first, and use reflective coatings only where people are not standing, such as drive aisles. My Topanga Willows study follows that order. [3] What I do not know # Limits of this entry I read the UCLA findings through a news report, not the report itself, so I state them at the level of detail the report gave. The Arizona figures are from one pilot, not a Los Angeles measurement. pages.x: Impervious surface | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Impervious surface Any hard cover that rain cannot soak through Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 4 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Impervious surface Rain on hard cover runs off. Concept sketch. Type Land-cover category Examples Roofs, roads, driveways, parking lots Effect More runoff, less infiltration [1] Linked risk More frequent, more severe floods [1] Fixes Bioswales , permeable paving Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is What happens to the water The heat link In the Valley What I do not know See also Notes What it is # An impervious surface is one that rain cannot pass through. The USGS gives the everyday examples: superhighways, streets, pavement, driveways and house roofs. [1] Land that is natural or planted can take in rain; hard cover sends it somewhere else. What happens to the water # In a forested watershed a significant share of rainfall is absorbed into the soil, stored as groundwater and released slowly to streams. When a watershed urbanizes and vegetation is replaced by impervious cover, there is less area where rain can infiltrate, so more runoff has to be collected by curbs, storm sewers and ditches and carried straight to streams. In a developed watershed much more water reaches a stream much more quickly, and the USGS states that severe flood events happen more often as impervious area grows. [1] The heat link # Impervious cover is also hard and dry, which is why it appears in the EPA’s list of heat island causes: hard, dry surfaces provide less shade and moisture than natural landscapes. [2] A parking lot is both problems at once, which is why I treat permeable paving and bioswales as part of the cooling design and not only the drainage design. In the Valley # Two Valley projects show the other direction. On Elmer Avenue in Sun Valley, a street with no pedestrian or stormwater infrastructure and frequent flooding was retrofitted so that bioswales and a buried infiltration gallery capture runoff from a 40-acre area. [3] The Tujunga Wash, a 13-mile tributary of the Los Angeles River, was channelized for flood control in the 1950s; [4] see riparian corridor for the greenway built beside it. What I do not know # Limits of this entry I do not have a percent-impervious figure for the Valley or for any site I have studied. For a site, I estimate it from aerial imagery, and I label it as an estimate. Contents Where it starts The river in the Valley Why it matters to a small place What I do not know See also Notes Where it starts # The Los Angeles River’s official beginning is the confluence of two channelized streams, Bell Creek and Arroyo Calabasas, in the Canoga Park part of Los Angeles, just east of State Route 27, which is Topanga Canyon Boulevard. [1] From there it flows about 51 miles through the San Fernando Valley, downtown Los Angeles and the Gateway Cities to San Pedro Bay at Long Beach, draining a watershed of about 827 square miles. [1] My first study site is on that same boulevard, though I have not traced where its runoff goes. The river in the Valley # The Sepulveda Basin is a flood-control basin and, with the Griffith Park area and the Willow Avenue estuary in Long Beach, one of only three stretches with a soft bottom. [2] The Tujunga Wash is a 13-mile urban tributary that was channelized for flood control in the 1950s. [3] Why it matters to a small place # Most of the river is a concrete channel designed to move floodwater out quickly, which is the same logic as a storm drain on a parking lot (see impervious surface ). The revitalization office reports that only the Sepulveda Basin and the Glendale Narrows presently support riparian habitat in the 32-mile project area. [4] A site that holds water and plants native trees is a small version of what the river lost (see riparian corridor ). I have not confirmed the 51-mile and 827-square-mile figures against a primary source, such as the Army Corps of Engineers or the county, so treat them as approximate. pages.x: Permeable paving | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Permeable paving Pavement that lets rain pass through to the ground below Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 4 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Permeable paving Rain passes through to a gravel base. Concept sketch. Type Paving system Kinds Pervious asphalt, pervious concrete, interlocking pavers, plastic grid pavers [1] Main benefit Less runoff, some filtering [1] Valley example Elmer Avenue, Sun Valley [2] Related Bioswale Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is Where I have seen it used Heat is a separate question A design judgment, labeled See also Notes What it is # Permeable paving is a family of surfaces that let rain and snowmelt seep through to underlying layers of soil and gravel. The EPA lists pervious asphalt, pervious concrete, interlocking pavers and plastic grid pavers. Besides cutting runoff, permeable pavements can filter pollutants and, by reducing the need for some conventional drainage features, reduce construction costs for residential and commercial development. [1] Where I have seen it used # The Elmer Avenue retrofit in Sun Valley installed 63 square feet of permeable concrete and 1,560 square feet of permeable pavers, alongside its bioswales. [2] Heat is a separate question # The EPA groups permeable surfaces under “cool pavements” because they can stay cooler by letting water evaporate. [3] But the cooling depends on moisture, and in a dry Valley summer I do not know how much of it is there. I treat permeable paving as a water measure first and a possible heat bonus second. For surface heat, see cool pavement . A design judgment, labeled # In my Topanga Willows study I put pavers under the parked stalls but keep asphalt in the drive aisles. That is my judgment about turning loads, not a rule I found in a source, [4] and it is the kind of detail an engineer would have to confirm. Permeable systems also need upkeep to stay open, and I have no cost or maintenance figures for Los Angeles. pages.x: Riparian corridor | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Riparian corridor The strip of living habitat along a stream or river Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 4 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Riparian corridor A bank with and without a planted edge. Concept sketch. Type Habitat and landscape type Where, in LA Sepulveda Basin; Glendale Narrows [1] Loss, LA River 90–95% of in-stream riparian habitat [1] Valley example Tujunga Wash Greenway, 15 acres [2] Related Los Angeles River Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is What was lost Sepulveda Basin Tujunga Wash Greenway Why a small site cares See also Notes What it is # A riparian corridor is the band of plants, soil and wildlife habitat beside a stream. Before the Los Angeles River was channelized, the areas next to it were riparian ecosystems with many native plant and animal species. [3] What was lost # The City of Los Angeles’s river revitalization office cites the California Coastal Conservancy: close to 100% of the original wetlands and 90–95% of in-stream riparian habitat in the Los Angeles River watershed have been lost to urbanization and channelization. Within the 32-mile river project area, the only places that currently support riparian habitat are the Sepulveda Basin and the Glendale Narrows, and both are stressed by exotic species, changed hydrology, dumped trash and encroaching development. [1] Sepulveda Basin # The Sepulveda Basin in the Valley is one of three places along the river with a soft bottom, and native willows dominate the banks between Burbank and Balboa Boulevards, though some non-native trees such as eucalyptus tower over the lower native shrubs. [4] The basin is also a flood-control basin, so the habitat and the engineering share the same ground. Tujunga Wash Greenway # A built example: the 1.2-mile Tujunga Wash Greenway turned an inaccessible right-of-way along a concrete flood channel into 15 acres of riparian habitat, 50 to 60 feet wide, planted with 1,100 trees and 18,000 shrubs and vines, all California natives. A naturalized streambed is fed by up to 325,000 gallons a day diverted from the channel. The project reports it infiltrates up to 118 million gallons of water a year from the channel, recharging the San Fernando groundwater basin, and cuts potential landscape water use by 70–80% by using native plants. [2] These are the project team’s reported figures from a case study brief, not independent measurements. Why a small site cares # My studies are not on river banks. But the Valley’s streets and lots drain toward these channels, so what I do with rain on a parking lot is the first link of the same system. See bioswale and impervious surface . pages.x: San Fernando Valley | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Valley context San Fernando Valley The inland basin north of the Santa Monica Mountains where my studies are set Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 5 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . San Fernando Valley A bowl ringed by mountains. Concept sketch. Type Urbanized valley, Los Angeles County Area About 260 sq mi [1] Population About 1.8 million (2023) [1] Record heat 121°F, Pierce College, Sept. 6, 2020 [2] Ringed by Santa Susana, Simi Hills, Santa Monica, Verdugo, San Gabriel ranges [1] Studies Heat , canopy Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents The setting Why it runs hot Water and ground Studies here What I do not know See also Notes The setting # The San Fernando Valley, “the Valley” locally, is an urbanized valley in Los Angeles County, north of the Los Angeles Basin. It covers about 260 square miles and had about 1.8 million people in 2023. It is bounded by the Santa Susana Mountains to the northwest, the Simi Hills to the west, the Santa Monica Mountains to the south, the Verdugo Mountains to the east and the San Gabriel Mountains to the northeast. [1] It includes a large part of the City of Los Angeles plus Burbank, Calabasas, Glendale, Hidden Hills, San Fernando and several unincorporated areas. [1] Why it runs hot # Because of its relatively inland position and other factors, summer days in the Valley are typically hotter, and winter nights colder, than in the Los Angeles Basin. [1] The extreme is Woodland Hills: on Sept. 6, 2020 the official site at Pierce College reached 121°F, the highest temperature ever recorded at an official station in Los Angeles County; it was reached at about 1:30 p.m. [2] [3] That is a single day, and a record at one station, but it is the reason I picked this part of the city. The mechanics of why built-up places stay hotter are in urban heat island . Water and ground # The Valley holds the headwaters and a long reach of the Los Angeles River , with tributaries such as the Tujunga Wash, and some of the clearest examples of retrofitting hard ground to take rain, such as the Elmer Avenue project in Sun Valley. [4] Studies here # My first study is a shopping center in Woodland Hills: Topanga Willows . [5] What I do not know # Limits of this entry The area, population and mountain boundaries come from Wikipedia, which I use for basic geography only. The Valley is not one climate: temperatures vary by neighborhood and elevation, and I have not compared stations. pages.x: Shade equity | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Trees and shade Shade equity Equal access to the cooling benefits of tree cover Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~2 min Sources 5 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Shade equity Same street length, two kinds of walk. Concept sketch. Type Planning concept Definition Equal access to the cooling benefits of tree cover [1] Facets Distributional, recognitional, procedural Tools Tree Equity Score, canopy maps Related Tree canopy Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is What the evidence shows Three kinds of fairness What I do not know See also Notes What it is # Shade equity is equal access to the cooling benefits of tree cover. [1] The idea is that shade is not a luxury: on a hot day it is the difference between a walk to the bus that is tolerable and one that is not, and it is spread unevenly. What the evidence shows # In Los Angeles, TreePeople’s canopy report found that much of the city’s canopy is “not where the people are,” and that some residents live virtually in a forest while many others live in virtually treeless environments. [2] The national picture is similar. The National Equity Atlas reports that across racial and ethnic groups in urban areas, people living below the federal poverty level have lower tree canopy coverage than those above it. [3] American Forests built the Tree Equity Score to prioritize investment where need is greatest. [4] A 2025 study modeled street trees in one low-income and one high-income Los Angeles neighborhood under two sets of spacing guidelines. Structural differences such as parcel size, intersection density and street width limited how many trees each neighborhood could host. Looser guidelines narrowed the gap in tree numbers , but substantial gaps remained in tree stature, a proxy for canopy. The authors conclude that shade equity may be hard to fix by changing guidelines alone. [5] Three kinds of fairness # The Union of Concerned Scientists argues that growing shade should account for more than where trees physically stand. Distributional equity is the map of who has trees. Recognitional equity means understanding the conditions and root causes, and engaging residents about their own goals and concerns. Procedural equity means transparent decisions and fair access to them. [1] I take that last point seriously for my own work. My studies are drawn from aerial imagery and public research, and they are concept studies. They are not a substitute for asking the people who use a place what they need from it. What I do not know # Limits of this entry The UCS piece is an advocacy-science blog post, and I read the Tree Equity Score and National Equity Atlas pages only as summaries. I have not checked the Valley’s shade distribution myself. The Messier study covers two neighborhoods, so I treat it as a case, not a rule. pages.x: Soil volume | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Trees and shade Soil volume How much root-friendly ground a tree gets, and why that decides whether lot trees live Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 2 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Soil volume A tree is half underground. Concept sketch. Type Planting design measure Guideline 2–3 cu ft of soil per 1 sq ft of crown spread [1] Field result Every tree with ≥1,500 cu ft was in good condition [2] Sample 1,127 trees, Walt Disney World [2] Related Tree canopy Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is A published guideline A field test What I do not know See also Notes What it is # Soil volume is the amount of uncompacted soil a tree’s roots can reach. In a parking lot it is the problem: a tree in a small paved island is, in the words of a Virginia Tech fact sheet, in a kind of pseudo-container. [1] A published guideline # The Virginia Tech fact sheet advises designing lot islands with as much soil volume as possible, ideally letting roots grow at least to the drip line, the edge of the crown, at maturity. It recommends 2 to 3 cubic feet of soil per 1 square foot of crown spread. [1] Worked example (my arithmetic) Take a tree whose mature crown is 30 feet across. The crown covers about π × 15² ≈ 707 square feet. At 2–3 cubic feet per square foot, that is about 1,400 to 2,100 cubic feet of soil, or a bed 3 feet deep and about 470 to 700 square feet. That is more than many parking islands provide, which is why soil, not the tree, is the hard part. A field test # A study of 1,127 parking lot trees at Walt Disney World found 81% in good condition and only 3% dead since planting, and that every tree in at least 1,500 cubic feet of soil was in good condition. Live oaks ( Quercus virginiana ) planted in groups did better than those planted singly. The authors also say existing planting recommendations were only imperfectly applicable to the site. [2] What I do not know # Limits of this entry The Disney lots are in Florida with different soil, species and irrigation than a Woodland Hills lot, and the 1,500 cubic feet result is for that sample. I do not know the soil under any Valley lot I have studied. A site would need a soil test and an arborist before I put numbers on a tree. h: Canopy is not the same as shade#
pages.x: Tree canopy | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Trees and shade Tree canopy The share of ground covered by tree leaves and branches, seen from above Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~2 min Sources 2 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Tree canopy Canopy is the view from above. Concept sketch. Type Land-cover measure Unit Percent of land under tree crowns LA County About 18% [1] City of LA About 25% [1] Data year Circa 2016 Related Shade equity , soil volume Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is It is not spread evenly Canopy is not the same as shade What I do not know See also Notes What it is # Tree canopy is the layer of leaves, branches and stems that cover the ground when you look straight down. “Percent canopy” is the share of an area under that layer. It is the standard way cities count their urban forest because it can be estimated from aerial imagery instead of counted tree by tree. An analysis of land cover data from about 2016 found that 18% of Los Angeles County and 25% of the City of Los Angeles was covered by tree canopy. [1] That 25% is the number I cite for the city in my studies. It is not spread evenly # The same report found that five census block groups, one in Pacific Palisades, one in Los Feliz, two in Brentwood and one in Shadow Hills, hold 18% of the city’s total tree canopy while less than 1% of the city’s population lives there. [1] The authors point to a cause: more affluent residents can afford the hill areas, which are better suited to trees and less densely developed. [1] The Union of Concerned Scientists repeats the same pattern, nearly 20% of the urban forest where 1% of people live. [2] That unevenness is the subject of shade equity . Canopy is not the same as shade # This is my own reasoning, not a sourced finding: a percent canopy figure averages over an area, but a person stands at one spot. A neighborhood can have healthy canopy in back yards and none over its bus stops. And a young tree counts as a dot from above while casting almost no shade for years. When I plan planting on a site I therefore ask where the shade lands, at what hour, over what people are doing, and how big the tree will be when it is mature. Getting a tree to maturity in a paved lot depends mostly on what is underground, which is the subject of soil volume . What I do not know # Limits of this entry The 18% and 25% figures come from one 2016-era land cover analysis and will have changed. I do not have a canopy number for the Valley as a whole, for Woodland Hills, or for any block I have studied. I would need the county’s canopy layer clipped to a site to state one. pages.d: Why built-up places run hotter than their surroundings, and the five causes that matter on a parking lot.
pages.x: Urban heat island | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Heat Urban heat island Why built-up places run hotter than the land around them Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~3 min Sources 3 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Urban heat island Same sun, different surfaces. Concept sketch. Type Climate effect Also called UHI, heat island Size, U.S. Day: about 1–7°F warmer. Night: about 2–5°F warmer [1] Two kinds Surface and atmospheric Main levers Shade, vegetation, reflective surfaces, less paving Seen in San Fernando Valley Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is Five causes Surface and atmospheric Why it matters In the Valley What I do not know See also Notes What it is # An urban heat island is a city or neighborhood that is measurably warmer than the less built-up land around it. The U.S. EPA summarizes the research this way: in the United States, daytime temperatures in urban areas run about 1–7°F higher than in outlying areas, and nighttime temperatures about 2–5°F higher. [1] The gap is usually measured as a difference between a city and its surroundings, so it depends on which surroundings you pick. A heat island is not the same thing as a heat wave. A heat wave is weather. A heat island is a built-in offset that rides on top of the weather, and it is largest on the calm, clear days when the weather is already dangerous. [1] Five causes # The EPA lists five, and each one shows up on an ordinary parking lot: [1] Fewer natural landscapes. Trees, plants and water cool the air by shading, by releasing water from leaves, and by evaporation. Hard, dry surfaces such as roofs, sidewalks, roads and parking lots do less of all three. Material properties. Conventional pavement and roofing reflect less solar energy and absorb and emit more heat than vegetation. Heat islands often build through the day and become stronger after sunset as that stored heat leaks out slowly. Urban geometry. Tall buildings and narrow streets trap heat and block wind. Waste heat. Vehicles, air conditioners, buildings and industry all release heat. Weather and geography. Calm, clear weather makes heat islands worse. Wind and cloud cover suppress them. Nearby mountains can block wind or redirect it. The first two are the ones a small site can change. That is why my studies spend their effort on tree canopy and on what the ground is made of ( impervious surface , cool pavement ). Surface and atmospheric # The term covers two different measurements. A surface heat island is how hot the ground and roofs themselves get, which is what a satellite sees. The EPA notes that on a warm day conventional roofing can reach as much as 66°F warmer than the surrounding air. [1] An atmospheric heat island is the warmer air, which is what a thermometer in the shade reads. The EPA says atmospheric heat islands vary much less in intensity than surface ones. [1] This matters for design claims. A pavement that is 15°F cooler at the surface has not made the air 15°F cooler, and a person standing on it feels more than air temperature (see cool pavement ). Why it matters # The EPA ties heat islands to three costs. Electricity demand for air conditioning rises about 1–9% for each 2°F increase in temperature. Higher demand means more fossil-fuel emissions, and more sun and heat means more ground-level ozone. And hot weather contributes to heat-related illness and death, with older adults, young children, low-income populations, people who work outdoors and people with chronic conditions at greatest risk. From 2004 to 2018 the CDC recorded an average of 702 heat deaths per year in the U.S. [1] In the Valley # The Valley is a plausible heat island host: it is inland, ringed by mountains, and summer days there are typically hotter than in the Los Angeles Basin. [2] Its all-time county record is a weather fact, not a heat-island measurement, but it shows the baseline a built-up block starts from: 121°F at Pierce College in Woodland Hills on Sept. 6, 2020. [3] What I do not know # Limits of this entry The 1–7°F and 2–5°F figures are a national range from a review of studies, not a measurement of the Valley. I have not found a published heat island magnitude for a specific Valley block, and I have not measured one. If I want to claim one for a study site, I need paired temperature readings at the site and at a shaded reference, taken the same hour. pages.x: A moonlit dark theme, and the circle that switches it on | Lab notes | Redrawn Valley ← Lab notes Theme A moonlit dark theme, and the circle that switches it on The site now has a second palette: warm orange-black paper, cream ink, and the brick accent turned into the blue-green of a lit window at night. It is a token swap, so every page, drawing and margin follows it. This is how I chose the colors, checked them, and made the switch feel like drawing a new sheet over the old one. By Nate Anderson Nov. 21, 2026 6 min read 4 sources Lab 7 of 7 01 Why a dark theme I read this site in a lot of places: a desk lamp, a bus, a bed. Bright cream paper is right for a printed site study and harsh for the last of those. The footer was already a dark band, and it was the part of the page I liked most, so the brief became: make the whole site feel like that band, warm and a little cozy, not cold grey. The rule I set was that a dark theme must be a change of tokens, not a second stylesheet. Every page already takes its color from variables, so a new set of values should re-color everything at once, including pages other people are editing right now. theme toggles on a page, in the header 1 pairings checked against WCAG AA 30 pages that load the theme script 46 flashes of the wrong theme on load 0 02 The palette Paper goes from cream #f6f1e7 to #17120d , a near-black with a clear orange cast, so it reads as a lamp-lit room and not as a screen. The raised surface for cards is a step lighter ( #211a13 ) and the sunk band a step darker ( #100c08 ), the same order as in the light theme. Ink flips to a warm cream, #f3e8d4 , which keeps the page from glaring. Paper #17120d Raised #211a13 Sunk #100c08 Ink #f3e8d4 Brick, moonlit #66c3c0 Moss, moonlit #9cc3a8 Slate, moonlit #86aed2 Footer band #0b0806 Brick, the one color that means “do something here,” became #66c3c0 , a pale turquoise: what a terracotta wall might look like with only moonlight on it. Moss and slate moved the same way, lighter and a touch cooler, because accents used as text have to rise off a dark page instead of sinking into it. Solid art fields are a separate set of tokens. A big block of pale turquoise would glare and would not carry the cream linework drawn on it, so the motif tiles use deeper fills ( --brick-fill , --moss-fill , --slate-fill ) that are identical to the accents in the light theme and muted in the dark one. The footer got its own --band tokens for the same reason: in the dark theme ink becomes cream, and a footer filled with ink would have turned bright. All 30 pairings I check meet WCAG AA when computed with the standard relative-luminance formula: 4.5 to 1 for text and 3 to 1 for large text and interface lines 1 . The lowest text pairing is faint caption text on a raised card at 6.6 to 1; the lowest interface line is the input border on a raised card at 3.9 to 1. The table is computed live in the palette sheet below. 03 The switch and the circle There is one button, a hand-drawn sun that turns into a hand-drawn moon, to the left of Search. It is two new icons in the same point-list source as the rest of the set, so they wobble like the others. The phone More sheet has a copy as its first row, with a small drawn switch, and the study pages, which have their own top bar, get it beside their Search link. The theme comes from the saved choice if there is one, and otherwise from the system setting. A tiny script in the <head> sets it before the page paints, which is why there is no flash of light on a dark page. The choice is saved in the browser and shared across tabs and embedded demos. When you press the button, the new theme grows out of it as a circle and keeps growing until it covers the page. It uses the View Transitions API 2 : the browser takes a picture of the old page, the theme changes underneath, and a growing circular clip-path reveals the new one. The radius is the distance to the farthest corner, so the circle always finishes by covering everything, and the duration scales with that distance between 0.7 and 1.1 seconds. Browsers without the API get a disc of the new paper color that grows the same way and then fades to reveal the page. With reduced motion on, the theme swaps instantly. The art that cannot read a variable is handled by one generated block: CSS data-URI drawings (the hand-drawn rules, wavy band edges and highlighter) are redrawn in dark colors by scripts/build_theme.py , and baked SVG attributes in older drawings are re-mapped to tokens by attribute selectors, which beat presentation attributes. 04 The decisions I made Swap tokens, not stylesheets Pages being edited by other threads keep working, and a new component gets a dark theme for free if it uses tokens. Cost Anything with a hard-coded color needs a one-time cleanup; I converted what I found and left the rest to the attribute remapping. Warm near-black, not neutral or blue-black The footer band the site started with is warm, and a warm black keeps the paper feeling of the light theme. Cost Warm darks are a little less crisp than neutral ones, so I kept text contrast well above the minimum. Brick becomes moonlit turquoise, everywhere The accent keeps its job (actions and the current page) and changes only its color, so nothing else needed to change. Cost Drawings that show a red awning now show a turquoise one, and a few sentences in the studies still say red. I left the text alone and flagged it. The footer stays the darkest thing on the page It is the reference I started from, so it has its own band tokens and does not follow ink. Cost Two more token families to maintain. A circle from the button, not a fade It ties the change to the thing you pressed and it can be smooth on a long page, because only a picture of the page is animated. Cost Needs a fallback and a reduced-motion path. I did not build the hand-drawn panel wipe, which was the alternative. 05 The palette sheet Both palettes drawn side by side, whatever theme you are in, with

This is how they are drawn, why the first version was thrown out, and the rules that keep new icons consistent. By Nate Anderson Nov. 21, 2026 5 min read 3 sources Lab 2 of 7 01 What the icons are for The site had text links and nothing else, and on a phone the bottom tab bar needs a symbol for every tab. I wanted a set that looks drawn rather than printed, small enough to ship as one file, and consistent enough that a new icon could be added by someone following the written rules. icons: 7 navigation, 16 interface, 15 topic 38 drawing grid 24 px line weight at 24px 1.9 px strokes in the logo 3 The set covers three jobs. Navigation icons sit in the header, the search button and the phone tab bar. Interface icons are arrows, chevrons, a check, a warning and similar. Topic icons start each row of the Field Guide, notes and studies indexes: heat, tree, shade, pavement, water, river, soil, sidewalk, bioswale, permeable paving, leaf, thermometer, pin, ruler and building. 02 How they are made Each icon is a short list of points on a 24 by 24 grid, written by hand in scripts/build_icons.py . The script then roughens the points with a seeded wobble, so the output is stable from run to run, and writes the sprite, the logo, the favicon and a names file that the gallery reads. I never edit the sprite directly: I edit the point list and run the script. A stroke can be a polyline with sharp corners, a smooth curve through points, a closed shape, or a circle. Any stroke can be marked as the accent, and any can lay a pale tint under it that is printed slightly off the line, like a marker that missed the edge. Linework uses currentColor , the accent uses one token, and the tint uses another, so a single CSS class recolors an icon (moss for trees, slate for water) without a second drawing. The first version was more detailed. I replaced it the same day with a set of two or three strokes per icon, a bolder line and a three-stroke logo, because fine detail does not survive at the sizes used beside body text. That is my judgment from looking at the icons at 16, 24 and 32 pixels. The gallery below is the second version. 03 The mark The logo is two ridgelines forming a valley. The ink line is the valley as it was drawn. The brick line beneath it is the same ridge redrawn, and a small brick sun sits low in the gap. That is the site’s whole idea in three strokes: look at a place, then redraw it. It has to read at 16 pixels because that is the favicon size, so the three-stroke limit is not decoration. In the header it sits left of the wordmark; the favicon is the same mark on a paper tile. Because both are made from the same point lists as the icons, they share the wobble. 04 The decisions I made Two or three strokes per icon, with one accent stroke on the meaningful part The accent is how an icon gets personality without a second color system: the door of the house, the leading edge of the pencil. Anything that needs more strokes is an illustration, not an icon. Cost Some topics (bioswale, permeable paving) are abstract at this size and rely on the label next to them. Never fill with solid ink Solid fills turn into blobs when the line is wobbly and break the sketch feel. Pale tints are allowed because they sit off the line and read as paper and marker. Cost Icons look lighter than a standard UI set next to bold text. Keep the source as point lists, not hand-edited SVG A point list is readable, diffable and easy to restyle; I could make the whole set bolder in one edit, which is what the second version needed. Cost Adding an icon means editing a Python file, which is a barrier for a contributor who only knows SVG. Linework follows the text color Using currentColor means icons work on paper, on the dark footer and in the active tab with no extra assets. Cost A single accent color per icon; no two-accent icons. Ship one sprite, referenced with use One request, cached, and every icon can be restyled in CSS. Cost External sprite references need HTTP, so icons do not appear if you open a page from disk. 05 The live gallery Every icon, at its real size, grouped the way they are used. Click an icon to copy its markup. The sizes and tab-bar sections lower on the page show how they scale. Live demo Open it as its own page → The gallery is generated by scripts/build_icons.py between its gallery markers. 06 What I could not verify Limits of this lab I judged legibility at 16, 24 and 32 pixels by eye on one screen. I did not test the icons with people, or on low-resolution displays. The icons are decorative and hidden from screen readers; the text beside each one carries the meaning. I have not tested that with a screen reader. The count of 38 is read from the generated names file on the day I wrote this and will change as icons are added. This is what each one is made from, how its colors are wired, and a sheet you can randomize. By Nate Anderson Nov. 21, 2026 5 min read 2 sources Lab 4 of 7 01 Where the pattern system started Before the seeded generator, there was a sheet of ten hand-built SVG motifs. I made it first because I wanted to check that the recipe from the reference library worked as original art before I wrote any code to randomize it. If the static motifs did not look right, a generator would only multiply the problem. motifs on the sheet 10 art-only accent colors proposed 5 flat colors per motif, plus ink and paper 2 to 4 color crossfade 1.2 s 02 What each motif is built from Each one comes from a habit I saw in the references, and each one has a use on the site. Grid-filled solids and split discs. Draw a shape in its flat color, then draw the same shape again filled with a 10 pixel graph-paper pattern at 70% ink. The grid stays on the shape, never the field. Used for hero art, dividers and stat cards. Overlapping circles. Three circles at 85% opacity with multiply blending, centers 70 pixels apart. Used for “evidence overlaps” figures. Set square and protractor. The drafting tool is the illustration: a triangle with a cutout and tick marks, a half disc with ticks every 2 degrees and one brick line as the measured angle. Contours. Nested wobbly rings, every fifth heavier, the same idea as the contour lines in the survey sheets. 2 Halftone. A staggered dot grid whose dot radius falls from one side to the other, for transitions between bands. Plan symbols. Tree canopies with a center dot, a dashed slate flow line, a scale bar, a north arrow and a double border like a drawing sheet. Moss for trees and slate for water, matching the design system. Three-tile collage. Two or three tiles side by side, each one thing, each on its own saturated field. This is the layout of the banners. 1 Pill diagram. Rounded pill labels joined by hairline arrows with pale fills, for process figures such as Site, Measure, Plan. 03 The decisions I made Wire every color as a CSS variable on the figure Each motif exposes --field , --a , --b and so on. Randomizing is then one line of script, and the generator that replaced this sheet could reuse the same idea. Cost The sheet itself uses literal hex values for a few fixed pieces, so it is a lab, not a model of token discipline. Propose five art accents instead of using only the interface colors Brick, moss and slate are too serious for decorative tiles; a field of sky, ochre, rose, kelly or periwinkle reads as the playful flat color the references use. They are for decoration only. Cost Adding colors to the system means updating DESIGN.md, which the pattern work did. Offer drift as a toggle, not a default Drift adds a slow six-pixel slide and the color transition. It is off until you press it, and it never runs under reduced motion. Cost On the sheet, motion is opt-in, which hides it from anyone who does not press the button. Keep the sheet, then build the generator The ten static motifs proved the look first. The generator in the pattern sheet article took them from fixed files to seeded art. Cost The two sheets overlap, and the static one is no longer the source of truth. 04 The live sheet Press Randomize colors to swap each motif’s colors from the palette, Reset to go back, and Drift for the slow motion. Live demo Open it as its own page → Ten vector motifs in Redrawn tokens plus the proposed art accents. 05 What I could not verify Limits of this lab The sheet is a design study. Its colors were chosen by eye against the reference sheets, and I did not run contrast checks because the motifs carry no text of meaning. The motifs are original drawings built from patterns that recur across the references, not traced from any one sheet. I list the sources I looked at so the influence is visible. pages.x: How the site moves: opening, wipes and handwriting | Lab notes | Redrawn Valley ← Lab notes Motion How the site moves: opening, wipes and handwriting The site used to animate only when you scrolled. Now it opens with a drawing, changes pages with a wipe of paper tiles, writes its headings in by hand and answers every click. Here is how that works, what I decided and what it costs. By Nate Anderson Nov. 21, 2026 5 min read 5 sources Lab 5 of 7 01 Why the site moves The site is made of sketches, and a sketch has a before and after: lines appear, then fill in. Pages that just snap from one to the next throw that away. I wanted every moment of waiting (the first load, a reload, a link click) to be a small drawing instead of a blank flash, and I wanted headings to look written rather than printed. The references pushed the same way. The tile collages, grid circles and squares from the reference sheets already work as flat, cut-out shapes, which makes them easy to move: a tile can grow, spin and shrink without any new art. things that play, in kinds 4 opening length, my setting 1.5 s page wipe, cover plus lift about 1.3 s script added to each page, one file 1 02 What plays, and when The opening. On the first visit of a browser session, and on every reload, a sheet of paper tiles covers the page. The logo draws itself, “Redrawn Valley” writes in, a tagline fades up, and the tiles shrink away from the center. It never blocks clicks on the page underneath, and a tap skips ahead. The page wipe. Following a link covers the page with tiles that grow outward from where you clicked, with the name of the section you are going to written on them. The next page lifts the same tiles from the same spot, so the two pages feel like one move. Handwritten headings. The page title writes in letter by letter, each letter bouncing on the Wobble font’s bounce axis before it settles, with a pencil squiggle drawn under it. Section headings do the same as they scroll into view. 1 Small answers. A click or tap leaves a quick pencil burst. Links get a wavy underline that sweeps in. Buttons spring and squish. Rows slide and their icons tilt. Rules draw on, and figures get crop marks in their corners for a moment. Back and forward buttons skip the opening and the wipe, because showing an animation on a page you are returning to feels slow. 03 The decisions I made Build the wipe myself instead of using the browser’s page transitions The View Transition API can fade between pages with almost no code, but it is newer, so older browsers get nothing, and it only crossfades snapshots. 2 A script that covers the page, remembers where you clicked, and lifts the cover on the next page works the same everywhere and can show tiles in our own colors. Cost Each navigation waits about 0.8 s before the next page starts to load, a delay the browser’s own transition would not add. Paint a paper sheet before anything else The script sits in the head and adds one CSS rule that paints paper over the page before the first frame, so there is no flash of unstyled content. A three second failsafe removes the sheet if anything goes wrong. Cost It is a blocking script, though a small one, and it hides the page during the opening. Hold the sheet in the top layer The tiles live in a manual popover, which browsers draw above everything including open dialogs, so a link chosen from the search dialog is still covered. 3 Browsers without popovers fall back to a very high z-index. Cost A top-layer sheet cannot be hidden by page code once it is open, so the failsafe has to remove it. Animate tiles with the Web Animations API Over a hundred tiles need staggered delays that depend on their distance from the click. Setting those per tile in code is simpler than generating CSS, and only transforms animate, so the browser can run them on the graphics card. 4 Cost On a very slow phone a hundred animated tiles may drop frames. I have not measured that. Turn everything off for reduced motion Under the reduced-motion setting none of this runs: no opening, no wipe, no dab, and headings stay plain text. Large movement across the whole screen is the kind of motion that setting exists to avoid. 5 Embed frames inside lab articles are off too, so a frame never covers its own article. Cost Those visitors never see the opening drawing. 04 The live demo Replay the opening, try the wipe from three starting points, write a heading again, click the grid for the pencil dab and change the speed. The effects play inside the frame, so they cover only the frame. Live demo Open it as its own page → Every effect on the site, one button each. 05 What I could not verify Limits of this lab All timings (1.5 s, 0.5 s, 0.8 s) are my own settings, tuned by eye on a desktop and a phone-size window. I did not measure frame rate on real phones. I tested in one Chromium build. Safari and Firefox should run it, since it uses long-standing APIs, but I have not seen it there. Each letter of a heading is its own element, and I gave each heading an accessible label with its full text. I have not tried it with a screen reader. pages.x: How every page got its own drawing | Lab notes | Redrawn Valley ← Lab notes Patterns How every page got its own drawing Every page and note on this site carries a banner drawn from a seed. This is how I got from a folder of reference sheets to fourteen original motifs, what I decided along the way, and a live lab where you can reroll one. By Nate Anderson Nov. 21, 2026 6 min read 4 sources Lab 1 of 7 01 Why generate the art at all The site started as words and a few diagrams. A study or a note with no picture at the top looks unfinished, but I had three rules in the way: no stock imagery, nothing glossy, and no copying another site’s art. Drawing a banner by hand for every page would also not scale, because every new note would need one. So the banners are generated from a seed. The page slug is the seed, which means the same page always gets the same drawing, and a different page gets a different one. That is the whole idea. Everything else in this article is about making the generated drawings look like they came from a sketchbook and not from a random-shape toy. motifs on the pattern sheet 14 colors: 6 interface, 5 art-only 11 layouts: banner, strip, card, square 4 between one tile shifting 5 to 10 s 02 What I studied I kept a reference library in the project files, outside the repo, and built contact sheets from it so I could compare many drawings at once. It has two parts. The first is screenshots of public pages from Anthropic’s site, taken on Nov. 20, 2026, for private study. 1 The second is public-domain drawings from the Historic American Buildings Survey and its sister programs, made for the National Park Service and held by the Library of Congress. I downloaded them from Wikimedia Commons, where each file is marked public domain, and the library’s own notes record that I checked that through the Commons API on Nov. 20. 3 Looking across the sheets, a few habits repeated. The “Building effective agents” hero is a three-tile collage: ink arcs on sage, a drafting compass on green grid paper, a weather-style contour map. 1 Anthropic’s designers describe the intent as soft beige, hand-drawn illustration and “the mark of the maker.” 2 The survey sheets contribute a different vocabulary: contour rings, tree canopies drawn as circles with a center dot, scale bars, north arrows, double-ruled borders. 3 From the contact sheets I wrote down a recipe: two to four flat colors per image plus ink and paper; each tile is one thing; a fine grid sits on a shape and never on the field; drafting tools appear as objects; and ink line weight stays constant inside one drawing. I did not trace anything. The reference pixels stay in the library, and the repo only holds motifs I drew in code. 03 The decisions I made Draw everything in code, from the recipe, not from the pictures The Anthropic art is copyrighted and the survey sheets are public domain but sheet-specific. Drawing each motif in code from the recipe keeps the site original and keeps the files small (one 35 KB script, not a folder of images). It also means every color is a CSS variable, so the art follows the design tokens. Cost More work up front, and no motif is as rich as a real engraved sheet. Seed the randomness with the page slug The same slug always draws the same banner, so a page does not change its look between visits and a bad composition can be fixed by changing one string. Pages without a topic draw from the full set. Cost I cannot hand-tune a single composition; I can only reroll the seed. Two palettes, with a firm rule between them Brick, moss and slate keep their interface jobs: action, link and water. Five extra colors (sky, ochre, rose, kelly and periwinkle), toned from the references, are for decoration only. They never carry text or meaning. Cost The art accents are not contrast-checked as text colors, so the rule is the safeguard. Keep the line weight constant and the grid on the shape This is the most visible habit in the references. It also keeps the generated art from turning into noise when a tile is small. Cost Some compositions look plainer than a freehand drawing would. Move slowly and rarely One tile shifts every five to ten seconds: a color crossfade, a disc turning into a rounded square, a needle swinging. It runs only while the art is at least 10% on screen and the tab is visible, and under reduced motion it stays still. Cost The motion is easy to miss, which is the point, but it means a screenshot never shows it. Bias the art by topic A data-topic leans the palette and motifs toward the subject: shade and trees toward moss and canopy plans, water toward slate and contours, heat toward brick and halftone, soil toward ochre. Cost The mapping is my judgment and is not tested on readers. 04 The live lab This is the same renderer the site uses, with the controls exposed. Type any seed, pick a topic and a layout, press Reroll for a random seed, and watch a tile change its color, shape or icon every few seconds. Pause drift freezes it. Live demo Open the full pattern sheet → Seed Topic Any Shade and trees Water and rain Heat and pavement Soil Layout Banner Card Square Strip Reroll Pause drift Grid-filled disc Drift: morphs into a rounded square. Overlapping circles Drift: the outer two spread apart. Protractor Drift: the needle swings. Contours Nested rings, every fifth heavier. Plan symbols Canopies, flow line, scale bar, north arrow. Halftone Dots shrink to one side. Rendered by assets/rds/motifs.js. Same seed, same drawing. The palette Six interface colors and five art-only accents. Hex values are the ones in the design tokens and in the motif code. paper #f6f1e7 paper-sunk #ece5d6 ink #1f1d1a brick #9c3d24 moss #2f4a3a slate #35506b sky #7ba3c0 ochre #be9661 rose #b17c83 kelly #4f9b60 peri #7c849f 05 What I could not verify Limits of this lab I judged every composition by eye at 375px and 1280px. I did not test the drift on a low-end phone or measure its battery cost; it pauses when off screen and under reduced

pages.x: The sources library: every citation, found by script | Lab notes | Redrawn Valley ← Lab notes Sources The sources library: every citation, found by script Every claim on this site has a numbered note, but the notes live on two dozen separate pages. The library collects all of them in one searchable list, shows every page that cites each source and the sentence it backs, and jumps you to the exact spot. By Nate Anderson Nov. 21, 2026 5 min read 3 sources Lab 6 of 7 01 What the library is for Evidence is the point of this site, but a reader who wants to know “where did 121°F come from, and who else used that source?” has to open pages one by one. I wanted one place that answers three questions fast: what are all the sources, which pages lean on each one, and what exactly did I use it for. sources, merged by link 99 citation markers read 266 pages that cite something 25 sources with a caveat I wrote 14 Those counts were read from the generated file on the day I wrote this. They will be different tomorrow, because nobody types the list. When I publish a page, the check script rebuilds it. 02 How it reads the pages The site grew three citation styles: field guide entries use rds-fn markers and an rds-notes list, notes and lab articles use rv-fn and rv-sources , and the studies use plain superscript links to a numbered list. Rather than force one format, scripts/build_sources.py looks for the thing they share: a link to an in-page #id , inside a superscript or a footnote class, that points at a list item. 2 The list item is the source; each link is one use. 3 Sources are merged by web address with the scheme, www , tracking tags and trailing slash ignored, so the same article cited from three pages becomes one entry with three places of use. For each use the script keeps the sentence the marker closes, the section heading above it, and the marker’s order on the page. It also reads the label I put beside a source (“Government page”) and any caveat I wrote (“seen only as a search excerpt”). Pull quotes that cite as plain text, like “[3]”, count as quoted uses. Types come from that label when it exists and otherwise from rules on the publisher’s address: a .gov address is Government, a known newsroom is News, and so on. Topics come from the words on the citing pages. Both are rules, not judgment, and I checked the output by reading the full list once and fixing the rules that put a state agency under “Other.” 03 Jumping to the exact sentence A link to a page is not enough when a page has eleven citations. Each use in the library links to page/#cite=note-lat.2 , which means “the second marker on this page that points at #note-lat .” A small script on every page, assets/rds/cite-jump.js , finds that marker the same way the build script did, scrolls to it, pulses it, and highlights the sentence it closes. A bar at the bottom lets you step through the other uses of that source on the page, jump to its entry, or go back to the library. The sentence is highlighted with the CSS Custom Highlight API, which styles a text range without wrapping it in new elements. 1 It works in current Chrome, Edge, Safari and Firefox, and on older browsers the whole paragraph is tinted instead. Some pages hide a marker at small widths (the field guide’s at-a-glance box on a phone), so the script falls back to the next visible use and says which one it is showing. 04 The decisions I made Read the pages; never keep a separate list A hand-kept bibliography goes stale the first time I forget it. The pages are the single source of truth, and the library is a view of them. A GitHub Action regenerates the file on every pull request, and the check script warns if it is stale. Cost A page that does not use numbered notes is invisible to the library, and two pull requests that both change the generated file can conflict. Jump links carry an order, not a hand-placed anchor Many markers have no id of their own, and adding one to each would mean editing every page and every future page. The order of a marker among those for the same source is enough to find it again. Cost If I add a citation above an existing one and do not rebuild, an old link lands one use off. The rebuild fixes it; the old address does not know. Search the claim, not only the title People remember “the 121 degree record,” not “Wigglesworth and Cosgrove.” The search covers the sentence each source backs, the section and the citing page, and shows the best matching sentence under the result. Cost The data file is about 115 KB, loaded once. That is fine for 99 sources and would need a smarter index at a few thousand. Show caveats, and do not rate sources If I wrote “I did not check its underlying data” beside a source, the library shows it and can filter to it. It does not score quality, because I would be inventing a number. Cost A source with no caveat is not thereby good; it only means I did not write one. Rules for types and topics Rules are predictable and easy to fix in one place. Asking a model or tagging by hand would be slower and would drift. Cost Some labels are wrong at the edges, such as a nonprofit report labeled as a report. 05 The live library Search a word, a number or a topic, filter by type, open a source to see every use, and press Jump to this claim . Press / to focus the search box. Live demo Open it as its own page → The data file is assets/sources.json, generated by scripts/build_sources.py. 06 What I could not verify Limits of this lab I read the generated list once for wrong types and topics. I did not measure how often the rules are wrong. The highlight is a visual cue only. The custom highlight does not carry meaning for screen readers, 1 so the bar at the bottom says in text which source and which use you were sent to. I have not tested it with a screen reader. I tested the jump links in one desktop and one phone-sized browser window, not on real phones or older browsers. A page that was edited after someone saved a jump link can land one

pages.x: Choosing a hand for the type | Lab notes | Redrawn Valley ← Lab notes Type Choosing a hand for the type Forty-six font entries screened for license, accents, size and legibility, six type directions built from them, and three ways to write text in. The research, the decision (Wobble, now live site-wide) and the live lab are all here. By Nate Anderson Nov. 21, 2026 7 min read 5 sources Lab 3 of 7 01 The question The site speaks in a serif, sets its interface in a sans, and uses a hand font for eyebrows, tags and notes. I wanted to find out whether a hand-drawn face could carry the site, and which one, without breaking three things I care about: free licenses, Spanish place names with accents, and text that stays readable at caption size on a phone. entries in the research table 46 under the OFL, 7 Apache 2.0 38 directions built and compared 6 ways to write text in 3 The table counts entries, and some entries group two or three related families, so the number of families screened is a little higher. The lab itself says about sixty. 02 What I screened and what I found For each candidate I recorded its license, the size of its Latin-subset file, and which of the glyphs I need are missing. The glyph check reads the font file’s own character map for the accented letters in Spanish place names, the degree sign, dashes, the multiplication sign, fractions and superscripts. Sizes are the woff2 files Google Fonts serves for the Latin subset, read on Nov. 21, 2026. 1 Almost everything is free for websites. 38 entries are under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, which allows self-hosting and embedding with no fee, and seven are Apache 2.0, which also does. 2 The one outlier is the Hershey single-stroke data I use for pen animation, which is free to use with credit. 4 Twenty entries made it into at least one direction and three more earned a place as annotation voices. Twenty-three were rejected, and the reasons cluster. Three have no accented letters at all (Nanum Pen Script, Gaegu and Edu SA Beginner), which breaks on a Spanish place name; Gaegu is also missing the degree sign and the dashes. Several are too thin or faint at caption size (Shadows Into Light, Coming Soon, Sue Ellen Francisco). Several are too wide, so headlines wrap (Gloria Hallelujah, Short Stack). Some read as a child’s card or a friendly app and not as a field sketchbook (Indie Flower, Schoolbell, Mali). The sketch-fill fonts turn to noise below 28 pixels. The complete table, with every font, license and verdict, is inside the lab below. 03 Six directions From the survivors I built six directions, each with a full hierarchy on a sample page so I could judge them in context and not as a specimen line. Field Notebook (Caveat, Kalam, Patrick Hand): looks written on site, and the most personal. Drafting Sheet : architect lettering for the plans. Marker and Brush : bold field-sign lettering. Typewriter Log (Special Elite, Courier Prime): a field log typed up, good where numbers lead. Hand-cut Serif (Fraunces): a serif with a hand in it. Wobble (Shantell Sans): one variable font whose letters can move. Hand fonts are good for titles, labels and notes and poor for long reading. They have small x-heights, uneven rhythm and thin strokes, and none of them read well for more than a few hundred words. That finding shaped every direction: the hand is for the display and the annotation, and the reading text stays a face built for reading. 04 The decisions I made Treat accents as a hard requirement The Valley has Cañada, Topanga and Tujunga on its maps, and a font that drops the ñ is a font that fails on the first page. Missing glyphs are a rejection, not a footnote. Cost It removed three otherwise attractive fonts from the shortlist. Choose Wobble (Shantell Sans) for the whole site My recommendation in the lab was Hand-cut Serif, with Field Notebook for titles, and I ended up choosing Wobble instead. County happened in Woodland Hills A 121-degree reading makes a headline. For a site study, the better question is what the thermometer can and cannot tell me about the block I am drawing. By Nate Anderson Nov. 20, 2026 5 min read 5 sources Note 1 of 5 01 One reading, and what it cannot tell you On September 6, 2020, the official weather station in Woodland Hills recorded 121°F. The National Weather Service said it was the hottest temperature ever recorded at an official station in Los Angeles County. The old record was 119°F, set in July 2006. 1 The same weekend, Burbank appeared to tie its own all-time record at 114°F. 1 The National Weather Service’s Los Angeles office described the Woodland Hills site as the one at Pierce College. 2 I started this site with a Woodland Hills sidewalk, so that number is not trivia to me. But one day is one day. A record is rare by definition, and I do not want to open a study by treating it as typical. What it does tell me is the ceiling: this part of the Valley can do that, and anything I draw for it has to survive that kind of day. Fig. 1 Official air-temperature readings from the L.A. Times report on the September 2020 heat wave, plotted on an axis that starts at 110 °F so the gaps are visible. Burbank’s reading was reported as appearing to tie its all-time record. Notice what the figure does and does not show. It shows three official readings. It does not show how hot any particular street was, because an official station sits in one spot and a sidewalk across town has different surroundings. Treat the number as a ceiling for the region, not a measurement of your block. 02 Heat islands are local, and canopy is what they track Some of the hottest spots in the Valley are not hot because of the Valley. They are hot because of what is on the ground. A study for the California Energy Commission used a calibrated weather model and observations to map neighborhood-scale heat islands across Los Angeles. Its authors include Haider Taha, who also ran the Pacoima cool pavement analysis I come back to in the next note. 3 The sentence in that report that matters most for my work is short. In the San Fernando Valley study area, the largest localized heat islands were associated with the lowest vegetation canopy cover. 3 The report’s model also put higher temperatures in the industrial and commercial areas running from near Chatsworth down through Canoga Park and Woodland Hills, and along major roads such as Sherman Way, Parthenia Street and Reseda Boulevard, with cool islands tied to areas of higher vegetation cover. 3 “In the San Fernando Valley study area, the largest localized heat islands were associated with lowest vegetation canopy cover.” Taha and colleagues, California Energy Commission, 2018 [3] That is one modeled study from 2018, and the report notes that near downtown a different factor, lower albedo, drove the largest local heat islands. 3 So I do not read it as “trees fix everything.” I read it as a reason to check canopy on my own block first, because in this part of the city missing canopy is exactly where the heat concentrates. 03 Shade is not spread evenly If canopy matters that much, the next question is where it is. TreePeople’s analysis of Los Angeles tree canopy found that about a fifth (18%) of the city’s tree canopy grows where only 1% of the city’s population lives. That canopy sits in just five census block groups, which together hold under a tenth (8%) of the city’s land, in Pacific Palisades, Los Feliz, Brentwood and Shadow Hills. 4 The same analysis lists the areas in highest need of protective canopy: southeast county along the Interstate 110 corridor, the northeast part of the San Fernando Valley, and northern Los Angeles County. 4 My reading of that, and it is my reading, not theirs: shade is not missing evenly, it is missing in specific places, and the places are not hard to find. A study that starts from the city average will be wrong about its own block. A study that starts by counting the trees within sight of the site will not. 04 Air temperature is not what a body feels A weather station reports air temperature. A person standing on a sidewalk also takes in sun on their skin and heat given off by the paving and the walls around them. The combined effect is usually described with a measure called mean radiant temperature, which the coverage of the Pacoima cool pavement study calls “a measurement of thermal comfort.” 5 Fig. 2 A weather station reports air temperature. A person on a sidewalk also takes sun on the skin and heat from the surfaces around them. Concept sketch, not a measurement. This is why a 2-degree change in air temperature can be much less important than whether you are standing in shade. It is also why I try not to quote air temperature alone when I describe a site. The next note works through a real test of that idea in Pacoima. 05 A ten-minute check for any block You do not need a lab to apply this. Before I propose anything for a block, I do a short check, and every step is something a person can repeat from a phone and a sidewalk. Count the crowns. Stand at the middle of the block and count the trees whose canopy actually overhangs the walk, not the trees on the lot behind it. Write the number down, including zero. Note the face. Which way does the walk face? A west-facing walk takes the afternoon sun, a north-facing one mostly does not. Orientation decides which hour is the problem. Look at what is under the feet. Dark asphalt, light concrete, or planting. The Taha report links low albedo to heat islands near downtown, so surface color is a real variable. 3 Stand in it. pages.x: A quarter mile is not the same walk in August | Notes | Redrawn Valley ← Notes Walking A quarter mile is not the same walk in August Transit planners measure how far people will walk. In a place that can hit 121 degrees, the better question is how much of that distance is in the sun. By Nate Anderson Nov. 20, 2026 3 min read 4 sources Note 5 of 5 01 The rule of thumb Ask a transit planner how far people will walk to a bus stop and you get a familiar answer: about a quarter to a half mile, or five to fifteen minutes. 1 Agencies write the number into their guidelines. The Boston region’s metropolitan planning organization, for example, describes a coverage guideline that gives residents access within a one-quarter-mile walk of transit in areas with more than 5,000 people per square mile. 2 I should be honest about the weakness of my sourcing here. The five-to-fifteen-minute rule is repeated across planning documents, and I could not trace it back to one original study. It reads like folk knowledge that got written down. That does not make it wrong, but it does mean I should not lean on its exact figures. 02 What a quarter mile is The distance itself is simple. A mile is 5,280 feet, so a quarter mile is 1,320 feet. If I assume a walking pace of 3 miles per hour, which is a round number I am choosing and not a measured Valley pace, that is about 4.4 feet per second, and 1,320 feet takes 300 seconds: five minutes. Fig. 1 A quarter mile is 1,320 ft however it feels. What changes is how much of it is in the sun. The tree positions are illustrative, not a real street. Concept sketch. Five minutes is nothing on a mild day. The problem is that the planning rule describes the walk as if every five minutes costs the same, and in the Valley they do not. 03 Distance is not the whole cost Research on how far people actually walk to transit suggests the rule of thumb is not a hard limit anyway. One study of trip distance and walking to reach public transit concluded that the distance people are willing to walk appears to be much higher than the frequently cited rules of thumb of 0.25 to 0.5 miles. 3 I have read only the abstract, so I cannot say how well it applies to Los Angeles. The distance is the same. The walk is not. Nate Anderson, this note That gap is why I do not think distance alone describes a walk. If willingness depends on the walk being tolerable, then shade, seating and surface can change who is willing to make it. I also know, from the first note in this series, that the Valley’s official record is 121°F. 4 On a day near that, five minutes at the same pace is not the same experience as five minutes in April. 04 A measure I want to try I want to add one number to my studies. I will call it the shaded share of a route. It is mine, and it is not an established standard, so read it as a proposal. The steps are simple enough that anyone could repeat them: Pick a route someone really takes, such as bus stop to storefront door. Walk it at a stated hour on a sunny day and mark each 100 feet as mostly shaded or mostly in sun. Report the shaded share as a fraction of the route, with the date, hour and orientation next to it. Draw the proposal and estimate the new share, labeled as an estimate. It is crude. Shade moves with the sun, and a pass at 3 p.m. says nothing about 11 a.m. But a crude, repeatable number beats a missing one, and it connects the distance people cite to the thing they feel. I have not collected any of this yet. Topanga Willows is the first place I would try it, because its walkway faces west. What I could not verify The origin of the five-to-fifteen-minute rule, and any Los Angeles-specific walking-distance data. The 3 mph pace is an assumption, so the five-minute figure is an estimate. I read only the abstract of the transit-walking study, and the Boston guideline is one region’s policy, not a national standard. pages.x: Shade beats paint, and Pacoima shows why | Notes | Redrawn Valley ← Notes Heat Shade beats paint, and Pacoima shows why Los Angeles coated 700,000 square feet of asphalt in a reflective surface and measured the result. The numbers are real. They also answer a smaller question than the one I care about. By Nate Anderson Nov. 20, 2026 3 min read 2 sources Note 2 of 5 01 What was tested In the summer of 2022, more than 700,000 square feet of dark asphalt in Pacoima, a neighborhood in the northeast San Fernando Valley , was covered with a solar-reflective coating. The project was a partnership between the local nonprofit Climate Resolve and the roofing and waterproofing manufacturer GAF, which supplied the coating. 1 Haider Taha, an atmospheric modeler, studied it for a year, and the results were published in the journal Environmental Research Communications . 1 One thing to say plainly: GAF funded the study. The reporting says the company had no role in its design, data collection, modeling or analysis, and the paper was peer reviewed. 1 I think that is worth stating because the coating maker also benefits when the coating works. I have not read the paper itself, only coverage of it, so I cannot check the method myself. 02 What it found During an extreme heat event, the coated area had air temperatures as much as 3.5°F cooler than the adjacent neighborhood. On sunny days the reduction was up to 2.1°F, and on summer nights up to 0.5°F. The coating also lowered surface temperatures by up to around 10°F. 1 An earlier city report on a Los Angeles cool pavement installation found it averaged 12.8°F cooler than nearby uncoated black asphalt. 2 Fig. 1 Pacoima, where over 700,000 sq ft of dark asphalt was coated in summer 2022. Air and surface temperatures are different quantities on different scales, so read each panel on its own. Values are the maximum (“up to”) reductions the study reported, not averages, except the city figure. Sources 1 and 2 . Those are real cooling effects, and I do not want to wave them away. A surface that is 10°F cooler stores and re-radiates less heat after sunset, which is probably why the biggest air-temperature effect showed up during the extreme heat event rather than on ordinary days. That last part is my guess at the mechanism, not something the study claims in the coverage I read. 03 The catch is what you measure Almost every number above is about the air or the pavement. Neither is a person. The coverage notes that some researchers have found reflected sunlight can raise how hot pedestrians feel, and Taha said his study indicated an “improvement in thermal sensation.” He also said mean radiant temperature, a measure of thermal comfort, “goes up and down. It’s not always cooler,” and that “The overwhelming effect is the cooling.” 1 Both statements can be true. A reflective street can cool the neighborhood and still push some light onto the person walking on it. “No change in surface will protect the body from heat as effectively as preventing sunlight from hitting the body in the first place.” V. Kelly Turner, UCLA Luskin Center for Innovation, quoted by Smart Cities Dive [1] Turner, associate director of UCLA’s Luskin Center for Innovation, wrote in an email to the reporter that shade can cool people by up to 30°C, or 54°F, in hot, dry environments, and that reflective pavement does not have a large effect on air temperature unless it is deployed widely, and even then the benefit is moderate. 1 Note that her 54-degree figure is a different kind of number from the bars above: it describes how much cooler a person can be made, not how much cooler the street gets. I kept them out of the same chart for that reason. 04 Where paint still makes sense I do not read this as “never coat pavement.” Turner herself says reflective pavement is an appropriate choice where it is hard to replace heat-absorbing surfaces with something like vegetation, and where the goal is to reduce what the surface materials add to the area’s heat. She calls it one tool among many for the regional heat island , not a substitute for protecting people from the sun. 1 That fits how many lots are laid out. A parking aisle has to stay open for cars. A tree cannot go in the middle of it. A coating could, in principle, do some work there, and shade trees go on the edges, in planting strips and between rows. For my own studies I treat it this way, as a proposal and not a result: Shade first: trees, canopies and buildings between the sun and the people. Surface second: where trees physically cannot go, consider a reflective coat, and say what I do not know about its cost and upkeep. I have not priced it. Always say which quantity a claim is about: air, surface or body. What I could not verify I read the Smart Cities Dive coverage and the snippet of the city report, not the journal paper or the full report. The 12.8°F figure is from one city installation and compares to nearby black asphalt; it is not the same test as Pacoima. I do not have cost, durability or maintenance numbers for the coating, so I make no claim about value for money. Keep reading Two more notes from the same notebook The hottest day on record in L.A.
