pages.x: The sidewalk is a promise Los Angeles made in court | Notes | Redrawn Valley ← Notes Streets The sidewalk is a promise Los Angeles made in court A settlement, a $1.4 billion program and three small numbers explain why a sidewalk looks the way it does, and why it is harder to plant than it looks. By Nate Anderson Nov. 20, 2026 4 min read 6 sources Note 4 of 5 01 How a settlement became a program Los Angeles runs a 30-year, $1.4 billion program to make its sidewalks accessible. The city launched it in December 2016. 1 The program exists because of a lawsuit, Willits v. City of Los Angeles , in which the plaintiffs alleged the city had failed to properly install and maintain accessible pedestrian facilities. 2 The city’s Bureau of Engineering says its Sidewalk Repair Program was initiated in response to the Willits settlement agreement. 3 One summary of the proposed agreement put the commitment at approximately $1.37 billion over 30 years. 4 The program is still being adjusted. The City Council approved a scoring system to prioritize repairs in January 2018, and in April 2026 approved a new Pedestrian Facility Severity Matrix. 1 Part of the program, the Access Request Program, makes repairs requested by or for people with a mobility disability who run into barriers such as broken sidewalks or missing or broken curb ramps. 1 The useful thing to take from this is that in Los Angeles a sidewalk is no longer leftover space beside the street. It is a legally tracked piece of infrastructure, and the reason is that people could not use it. 02 The three numbers that shape a sidewalk The federal Access Board’s guidelines for the public right-of-way set the technical rules for what counts as an accessible route. The board issued the final rule in August 2023. 5 I will say now that these are guidelines, and I have not checked which version Los Angeles’s own standards currently point to, so I use them here as the clearest published statement of the dimensions, not as the city’s legal requirement. These are the three that matter most for what I draw: Width. The continuous clear width of a pedestrian access route is 48 inches minimum, not counting the curb. Where it is narrower than 60 inches, passing spaces of 60 by 60 inches must be provided at intervals of 200 feet at most. 6 Slope across the walk. The cross slope of a pedestrian access route outside a crosswalk is 1:48, or 2.1%, at most. 6 Steps between slabs. Grade breaks must be flush. Changes in level of ¼ inch or less may be vertical. Between ¼ and ½ inch they must be beveled no steeper than 1:2, and above ½ inch up to 6 inches the slope can be 1:12 at most. 6 Fig. 1 The three numbers that shape most sidewalk design under the federal guidelines: clear width, cross slope, and the step between slabs. A tree trunk or pole inside the 48 in is a defect, not a feature. Concept sketch. “Changes in level of ¼ inch (6.4 mm) maximum shall be permitted to be vertical.” U.S. Access Board, Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines, R3 [6] 03 Why this matters for shade Put the two notes together and a tension appears. A tree needs lots of soil (see the previous note), and the sidewalk needs 48 clear inches with no vertical step bigger than a quarter inch. Roots lift slabs. Trunks grow into the clear width. Both are hard to design around when the strip is narrow, and it is why “just plant a tree” is never a complete drawing. I need to be careful not to overstate that. I know roots are a common reason for lifted slabs, but I have not found Los Angeles data on what share of the city’s sidewalk defects come from tree roots, so I cannot say how big the problem is here. I would not trust anyone who gave me a percentage without a source. What I take from it as a design rule is concrete. For each tree I propose, my drawing should show the clear width left beside it, the soil it will reach, and what happens at the slab joint if a root lifts it. If I cannot draw those three things, I should say so and not label the tree as solved. 04 What I check before I draw a bench or a tree A sidewalk plan is mostly a list of things that cannot be in the way. Here is the short version of how I now read a site, using the dimensions above. Measure the clear width at the narrowest point, which is usually a pole, a hydrant, a signal box or a tree guard, not the middle of the slab. Look along the joints for steps. A step taller than the quarter inch the guidelines allow to stay vertical is a defect to note, and one beyond half an inch needs a ramped transition. 6 Check whether the walk is public. On Topanga Canyon Boulevard in my first study, the planting strip is public right-of-way, so anything there is a request to the agencies, not something an owner can just build. Add a bench or tree only where the 48 inches survive. If they do not, the furniture goes on private land behind the walk. 05 What I do not know What I could not verify I read the program’s own pages and the Access Board’s text, not the settlement agreement. I have not found how many miles of sidewalk have been repaired so far, or whether the program is on schedule. I have not checked which accessibility standard the city currently enforces; the numbers above are the federal guideline text. That list is also my to-do list for a longer note. A real answer to “is the program working?” needs the city’s progress reports, and I have not read them. pages.x: A shade tree is a soil problem first | Notes | Redrawn Valley ← Notes Trees and soil A shade tree is a soil problem first Everyone agrees the Valley needs more trees. Almost nobody draws the hole they have to grow in. The arithmetic is simple, and it changes what a street can hold. By Nate Anderson Nov. 20, 2026 4 min read 4 sources Note 3 of 5 01 The rule of thumb everyone repeats If you ask how much soil a big street tree needs, you hear a number: about 1,000 cubic feet. It is a long-repeated rule of thumb. DeepRoot, a company that sells soil-cell systems for street trees, calls it “a helpful rudimentary rule of thumb” and says the industry has moved beyond it. 1 A seller of tree-soil products has a reason to say more is better, so I treat that as a source for the existence of the rule and not as proof of the right number. A neutral reference is the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency’s stormwater manual, which lists example minimum tree soil volumes from different jurisdictions. Among them: 30 cubic meters (1,059 cubic feet) of soil per tree, and 20 cubic meters (706 cubic feet) per tree when the volume is shared between trees. 2 I do not know which jurisdictions those two entries belong to, only that they are listed as real requirements. 02 A second way to get the same number The American Society of Landscape Architects offers a different route: trees need about 1.5 to 2 cubic feet of loam soil per square foot of the area under their mature canopy . 3 That makes the volume depend on how big the tree gets, which is more honest than one number for every species. Try it with a tree that has a 30-foot crown. I picked 30 feet as an example, it is not a measured tree. A circle 30 feet across has an area of about 707 square feet (π × 15²). At 1.5 to 2 cubic feet per square foot, that is roughly 1,060 to 1,410 cubic feet of soil. That lands right around the 1,000-to-1,059 figures above, which is the reason I trust the order of magnitude even though I do not trust any single rule to the last foot. A tree is a bet on how much soil it can reach. Nate Anderson, this note The academic version of the idea goes back at least to 1991, when Lindsey and Bassuk published a method for specifying soil volumes to meet the water needs of mature street trees and trees in containers. 4 I have read its title and abstract page, not the full paper, so I am citing it for the existence of the approach, not for its numbers. 03 The tree well next to it Now compare that with the hole most sidewalk trees are given. I do not have a measured sample, so I use an assumption and label it: a small tree well of 4 by 4 feet, dug 3 feet deep. That is 48 cubic feet. Against a 1,000-cubic-foot target it is about one twenty-first, and against the 1,059 figure about one twenty-second. Those ratios are my arithmetic on my assumed well. Fig. 1 Plan view at one scale: the soil a mature shade tree is commonly said to need, set against a small tree well. The 1,000 cu ft figure is a rule of thumb, and 48 cu ft is my assumed size for a small well. Arithmetic: 1,000 ÷ 3 ft = 333 sq ft, about 18 × 18 ft. Concept sketch. Spread over 3 feet of depth, 1,000 cubic feet needs about 333 square feet of soil surface, which is roughly 18 feet by 18 feet. The picture matters more than the ratio. A sidewalk planting strip is often only a few feet wide, so the soil a tree needs does not fit under the strip. It has to run under the paving, the parking lot or the road edge, where it competes with everything else buried there. 04 How I would check a real strip If I were sizing soil for a real planting strip, I would work in this order, and I would stop at the first step I could not complete. Measure the strip. Width, length and the clear width left on the walk beside it. The surface area available is the first limit. Find what is below. Request utility information and look for as-built drawings before assuming any depth is free. Pick a tree and its mature crown. Then apply the 1.5 to 2 cubic feet per square foot rule from the landscape architects as a first pass. 3 Compare with what fits. Multiply the strip’s area by a usable depth. If the answer is far under the target, the choices are a smaller tree, shared soil with a neighbor, or a different location, not a hopeful drawing of a large tree. The honest result is often “a smaller tree than I wanted.” That is still better shade than a large tree that dies young in a small hole. 05 What that does to a plan This is the part I find most interesting as someone heading toward civil engineering. The tree is the easy line on the drawing. The hard parts are underneath: Utilities. Water, sewer, gas and electric lines already occupy the ground. Before drawing any soil volume I would need a locate and as-built drawings, not an assumption that the ground is empty. Sharing. The 706-cubic-foot shared figure suggests one way out: a continuous soil trench under a row of trees, instead of separate pits. That is my reading of the shared-volume entry, and I have not seen it detailed for Los Angeles. Paving on top. If the soil is under a walk or lot, the paving has to carry loads over it, which is a structural design question, and the reason systems like soil cells exist. I have not engineered that and am not claiming a solution. Width on the surface. The tree and its tree guard cannot narrow the walkway below the accessible minimum. The next note covers that rule. Topanga Willows, my first study, is where I ran into this: a long west-facing storefront, one small tree, and a planting strip that belongs to the public right-of-way. so it is the first place to check whether this arithmetic holds up on a real site. Read the study → What I could not verify The 4 × 4 × 3 ft well is my assumption of a small well, not a surveyed one. I do not know the soil-volume requirement in the City of Los Angeles code, and I do not claim one here. Fallbrook Center is a 1,120,000 square foot open-air center on the west side of Fallbrook Avenue, anchored by Ralphs, Walmart, Trader Joe’s and Sprouts [1] . The owner’s site plan lists 52 units. Its mobile-location vendor counts 11.1 million visits and 1.2 million visitors a year, and ranks it fifth among shopping centers within 15 miles, behind Westfield Village at Topanga, Northridge Fashion Center, Westfield Topanga and Century City [1] . That is a vendor figure in a leasing brochure, so I read it as a sign of scale, not a precise count. Divided by 365 it is about 30,000 visits a day, my arithmetic. It began as Fallbrook Square in the 1960s, was enclosed and renamed Fallbrook Mall in 1986, then opened back up as an open-air center in 2003 [3] [4] [5] . The Wikipedia page and the Times disagree on the opening date (1963 versus 1964) and the Times and the Daily News disagree on the year it was built (1964 versus 1966). I only need the decade. Why this section. A shopping center this size has many places to study. I chose the edge for three reasons. First, it is the part of the property the public owns a view of: 1,770 feet, about a third of a mile, facing a street that is about 100 feet wide. Second, an edge can be redesigned without touching a single store, which makes it a realistic first move for an owner. Food and groceries are already a few minutes away on foot. This study asks what the corner itself would need to be somewhere people choose to stay, and draws six moves to get there. Study 03 · at a glance Ventura & Topanga Corner Location 22001 Ventura Blvd, Woodland Hills, CA 91364, at Topanga Canyon Blvd [1] Site type Freestanding retail building, 5,437 sq ft on a 0.22-acre lot, built 1980 [1] Focus Walking, shade, places to sit, a safer crossing, small shops Methods Listing data for size, lot and distances Parking, sidewalk and bus rules as targets Research review, 16 cited sources Plan, section and crossing drawn from dimensions Status Concept study. Not commissioned by the owner. By Nate Anderson Date November 2026 Field guide Urban heat island Tree canopy Soil volume Shade equity Right-of-way 10 sections · 4 parts · 16 sources What is real here The address, building size, lot area, year built, traffic counts and the distances to nearby food and groceries all come from one broker listing. [1] The parking ratio, sidewalk clearances, bus shelter width and head-start signal timing come from City, FHWA and Metro documents. The heat and tree research is cited in section 04. What is estimated Everything drawn. The lot is drawn as 100 by 96 feet because that has the right area, and the real lot is probably not a rectangle. The building is 78 by 70 feet (5,460 sq ft against the listing’s 5,437), the sidewalks are 10 feet, and the doors, trees, plaza and shops are my proposal. Expect any dimension to be off by 10 percent or more. I could not reach the City’s zoning map or the County Assessor from where I worked, so zoning and parcel number are not verified (see section 10). Part 1 of 4 The site What is there and what is around it 01 The site A building in the middle of its paving, on a corner of two 40,000-car streets The lot is about 9,600 square feet. Slightly more than half of it is building. The site is 22001 Ventura Boulevard, a freestanding retail building of 5,437 square feet on a 0.22-acre lot, built in 1980. [1] It is listed for lease as a whole building, with parking on its side and rear. [1] The listing was last updated on October 27, 2026 and says the space is available immediately, with a sublease running through April 30, 2032. [1] I treat the building as open to change, but I do not know who holds the lease or what the owner wants, and I did not contact anyone. Half an acre would be 21,780 square feet, so 0.22 acre is about 9,600. If the building is one story, which the listing does not say, it covers about 57 percent of the lot (5,437 divided by 9,583). That leaves roughly 4,100 square feet for parking, walkways and landscape. Fig. 1, in section 05, starts from this plan and adds one move at a time. The listing gives traffic counts of 41,000 vehicles a day on Ventura and 40,000 on Topanga Canyon. [1] Those are a broker’s figures, I have not matched them to a City or Caltrans count, and a car that turns here is counted on both streets. I use them only for scale: this is a corner people pass at speed far more often than they stop at it. 02 The neighborhood Ten places to eat and two grocers are inside a five-minute walk So people already come here on foot. The open question is where they would sit. Dunkin’ place to eat 0.05 mi Subway place to eat 0.06 mi Monty’s Steakhouse place to eat 0.06 mi Chipotle place to eat 0.08 mi Curry Up Cafe place to eat 0.11 mi Noah’s Bagels place to eat 0.11 mi Jamba place to eat 0.12 mi Fatburger place to eat 0.13 mi Ralphs grocery 0.13 mi Urban Plates place to eat 0.15 mi Corner Grille Korean Fusion place to eat 0.16 mi Sprouts Farmers Market grocery 0.20 mi Whole Foods Market grocery 0.53 mi Trader Joe’s grocery 0.79 mi Smart & Final grocery 0.80 mi place to eat grocery 0.25 mile, about 5 minutes at 3 mph Fig. 2 plots every restaurant and grocer in the listing’s points-of-interest list, by the listing’s own distance to the building. [1] All ten places to eat are within 0.16 mile, and two grocers, Ralphs at 0.13 and Sprouts at 0.20, are inside a quarter mile. At a walking pace of 3 miles an hour, a quarter mile is five minutes (my arithmetic). The same page reports a Walk Score of 90, a Transit Score of 43 and a Bike Score of 55. [1] What the listing cannot tell me is which direction each place lies, whether the walk to it is pleasant, or what the corner offers once you get there. It also lists only some places. I read this as evidence that the foot traffic exists, not as a count of it. I found no public plaza or park in that list within a quarter mile, but that is the listing’s list, not a survey. Part 2 of 4 The evidence The rules that bind it and what has been measured elsewhere 03 The rules At today’s parking ratio the lot cannot hold the stalls this building would need That makes every stall a trade, and it shapes every move in this study. Ventura Boulevard has its own set of rules, the Ventura-Cahuenga Boulevard Corridor Specific Plan, which covers the Woodland Hills stretch of the street. Where it is stricter than the general City code it prevails. [2] For commercial uses other than offices it asks for at least one parking space per 250 square feet of floor area. [2] For 5,437 square feet that is 21.7, so 22 stalls. Here is why that matters. A standard stall is about 9 by 18 feet, which is my assumption, so 22 stalls need at least 3,564 square feet for the stalls alone, out of the roughly 4,100 square feet of paving. That would leave about 540 square feet for a drive aisle, and a drive aisle alone needs more. So I do not think the lot meets the ratio by itself today.
